# @aponiajs/devtools

> The opt-in devtools surface for a running AponiaJS application. A disabled registration mounts nothing; an enabled one mounts an Elysia plugin that runs at `onStart`, after every route has mounted, and serves a loopback HTTP API.

The package is a leaf: nothing in the framework depends on it. An application imports `DevtoolsModule.register({ enabled })` and decides for itself whether the devtools mount at all — the framework never reads an environment variable on the application's behalf.

## What this package exports

- [DevtoolsModule](https://github.com/aponiajs/aponiajs/blob/release/alpha/packages/devtools/src/module/devtools-module.ts): `register(options)` builds the module an application imports; a disabled registration is inert.
- [DevtoolsOptions](https://github.com/aponiajs/aponiajs/blob/release/alpha/packages/devtools/src/module/devtools-module.types.ts): the required `enabled` switch, the optional loopback `port`, the optional `capture` policy `/requests` records under — every option an opt-out, with `redact` empty by default because the tool shows what arrived — and the optional `logger` whose lines `/logs` records, the same object the application gives `AponiaFactory.create`, because the framework never exposes the logger it builds for itself.
- [startDevtoolsServer](https://github.com/aponiajs/aponiajs/blob/release/alpha/packages/devtools/src/server/devtools-server.ts): starts the loopback server for one boot, or answers `undefined` when the port is taken.
- [routeRequest](https://github.com/aponiajs/aponiajs/blob/release/alpha/packages/devtools/src/server/request-router.ts): the pure dispatcher every request goes through.
- [AponiaMetaPayload](https://github.com/aponiajs/aponiajs/blob/release/alpha/packages/devtools/src/endpoints/payloads.types.ts): the `GET /__devtools/meta` payload, including the `contract` version a client checks first.
- [AponiaGraphPayload](https://github.com/aponiajs/aponiajs/blob/release/alpha/packages/devtools/src/endpoints/payloads.types.ts): the `GET /__devtools/graph` payload, the compiled module graph with no `routes` key.
- [AponiaRoutesPayload](https://github.com/aponiajs/aponiajs/blob/release/alpha/packages/devtools/src/endpoints/payloads.types.ts): the `GET /__devtools/routes` payload, every route the application answers with the binding that serves it.
- [AponiaFlowPayload](https://github.com/aponiajs/aponiajs/blob/release/alpha/packages/devtools/src/endpoints/flow.types.ts): the `GET /__devtools/flow` payload, the stages each mounted route passes through and the filters that answer when it throws.
- [createLogBuffer](https://github.com/aponiajs/aponiajs/blob/release/alpha/packages/devtools/src/logging/log-buffer.ts): the bounded log stream `/logs` publishes, and the capacity it retains.
- [tapLogBuffer](https://github.com/aponiajs/aponiajs/blob/release/alpha/packages/devtools/src/logging/log-tap.ts): records everything a `LoggerService` writes into a buffer, patching the logger in place and answering the stream that records it — one logger, one stream — or `undefined` when nothing could be installed on the logger, which is why a logger it cannot patch is never published as one.
- [AponiaLogsPayload](https://github.com/aponiajs/aponiajs/blob/release/alpha/packages/devtools/src/endpoints/payloads.types.ts): the `GET /__devtools/logs` payload, the entries after one cursor and the cursor to poll from next.
- [AponiaRequestsPayload](https://github.com/aponiajs/aponiajs/blob/release/alpha/packages/devtools/src/endpoints/payloads.types.ts): the `GET /__devtools/requests` payload, the requests the application answered after one cursor and the cursor to poll from next.
- [AponiaAotPayload](https://github.com/aponiajs/aponiajs/blob/release/alpha/packages/devtools/src/endpoints/aot.types.ts): the `GET /__devtools/aot` payload — the graph the container compiled and the boot's verdict on the generated invoker artifact, beside a build's per-handler verdicts for the project the server was started in.
- [createRequestBuffer](https://github.com/aponiajs/aponiajs/blob/release/alpha/packages/devtools/src/requests/request-buffer.ts): the bounded request record `/requests` publishes, and the capacity a registration retains.

## Behavior a consumer can rely on

- A disabled module registers no provider, mounts no plugin, and opens no socket.
- An enabled module registers an `ElysiaPluginModule`, so its plugin runs at `onStart` — after every route has mounted.
- `onStart` fires on `listen()`. An application that only calls `handle()` publishes nothing and is unaffected.
- The bind address is `127.0.0.1` and is not configurable.
- A port that is already bound is reported under `Devtools` and never fails the boot: the application answers its own routes without the devtools server.
- The devtools socket stops when the application is closed, so a restart binds a fresh one.
- `GET /__devtools/meta` reports the contract version, the release that booted the application, the Elysia installed in the application's own tree (`null` when there is none), and which release supplied each artifact the boot adopted (`null` for one it did not).
- `GET /__devtools/graph` reports the graph the application compiled: its modules with their imports, controllers, providers, dependencies and exports, and its WebSocket gateways with their events. It describes the descriptor artifact's graph when the boot adopted one and the lowered decorated classes otherwise, and it carries no routes.
- `GET /__devtools/routes` reports the routes the application answers, read from the mounted table when the request arrives, so a route mounted after the boot appears too. Each route carries the method and path the table states, the module, controller and handler the boot recorded, the context fields its handler binds, and `source`: `"generated"` for a build-time invoker, `"compiled"` for the running platform's own binding, or `null` when no boot recorded the route. A route no record describes reports empty names rather than guessed ones.
- `GET /__devtools/flow` reports the stages each mounted route passes through and the filters that answer when it throws, read from the mounted table when the request arrives. The stages a route's hooks and schema state come from that table; the stages its guards and interceptors state come from the compiled plan, because the platform lowered them into one `beforeHandle` and one `afterHandle` where their order is no longer legible, so each names the class it runs. A compiled hook is published as its parts and never as a hook stage, and a contributed hook is identified by the checksum Elysia stamps rather than by a plugin name the route does not carry. Filters are a list beside the stages, never a stage in the chain. One limitation is stated rather than hidden: an interceptor half declared as a class field (`interceptBefore = () => {}`) does not appear, because the stage a route runs is decided from the class tokens the plan carries, read through their `prototype` — the object an instance's methods resolve through — while a half declared as a prototype method is reported in full.
- `GET /__devtools/logs?since=<cursor>` reports what the application logged: the registration patches the logger the application passes as `logger` — the same object it gives `AponiaFactory.create` — and records every line into a bounded buffer from the moment the module registers, so the lines a boot writes about itself are included. An answer carries `{ cursor, entries }` with each entry shaped `{ level, context, message, timestamp }`. A cursor older than the retained window answers what is retained and one ahead of every write answers nothing, so a poll is never an error, and the cursor never goes backwards. A registration with nothing to record from — an omitted option, `logger: false`, a level array the platform builds a logger from, or a logger object whose first level refuses the patch — serves no `/logs` rather than an empty stream, because an empty stream would announce that nothing is being logged while an application that handed the factory a logger logs normally. A logger that accepts one level's patch and refuses the next one's is not that case: a level was patched before the refusal, so the stream is served and records the levels the tap reached. The payload does not say which levels are missing — an entry states only the level it was written at — so a stream that never carries `debug` cannot be told from one whose `debug` lines were never written.
- `GET /__devtools/requests?since=<cursor>` reports the requests the application answered. Everything is recorded by default and every option under `capture` is an opt-out, never a permission: an entry carries the `method`, the `path` — the route pattern that matched, or the path that arrived when none did — the `url` as it arrived, the `status`, the `durationMs`, the `timestamp`, the request's `headers`, and the `body` the route parsed, truncated at `capture.bodyLimit`, while a body this package cannot serialize is stored as `[unserializable]` rather than left out, because a missing `body` would read as a request that carried none. `error` is what the answer published and never the exception: present on a `5xx` whose Problem Details body the tool can read, absent on a `4xx`, which is an answer rather than a failure, and absent where there is nothing to read — an unhandled failure the platform mapped, and a `5xx` a handler built itself. A token passed as a query parameter is captured in `url`, which is a fact about the record rather than a defect in it: `capture.redact`, empty by default, replaces named headers with `[redacted]`. `durationMs` is measured from the moment the request reached this package's arrival hook to a reading taken after this package has read the route, the status, and the parsed body, so this package's own synchronous reads of the request and the answer are inside it and the field is not "the time the application spent on the route". A request that matched no route has no route identity — `path` carries the path that arrived, and `/routes` is the table that tells the two apart. The record belongs to one application and one boot: two applications in one process, and two registrations, keep their own windows, and a second `listen()` begins a new empty one rather than extending the window a socket that is gone was serving. A registration told to capture nothing still serves `/requests`, answering an empty record rather than no endpoint. An answer carries `{ cursor, entries }` under the `/logs` rules, so a poll is never an error and the cursor never goes backwards.
- `GET /__devtools/aot` reports what a build decided beside what the boot did with it. `graph` — the root the container compiled — and `invokers` — the boot's verdict on the generated invoker artifact, with the refusal's own sentence and no `reason` key at all when there was no refusal — come from the boot record, so they are answered whether or not a project is on disk. `controllers` comes from `@aponiajs/cli`'s analysis of the project the process was started in — the source root `aponia.json` names, walked the way `aponia build` walks it — and gives each handler's verdict: `"generated"` when the emitter renders an invoker for it, `"compiled"` when it declines and the running platform keeps compiling it, with the emitter's own reason. A handler is one property key, however many route decorators it carries. The analyzer is imported on the first request to this endpoint and never at boot, and its result is cached for the life of the process, so an application that never polls this endpoint never loads `ts-morph`. A project the analysis cannot read — no `aponia.json`, no controller under the source root, a source root outside the project, two controllers sharing one class name, an analyzer that would not load — leaves `controllers` empty and reports the reason once under `Devtools`, while the boot's own facts are still answered. A project whose every handler was declined still reports those verdicts, because they are what the endpoint exists to explain. The endpoint is served only for a record that states the two boot facts it publishes; a record that does not is answered with `404` while every other endpoint this server serves keeps answering. That is a different failure from a project the analysis cannot read, which still answers with the boot's half and an empty `controllers`.
- Every endpoint is a `GET`. Any other method answers `405` before the path is read, and a path the server does not serve answers `404`.
